**All five methods are coded correctly.** Each agrees with an independent solver of its equations to rounding
error and, where tested, returns a truth it can represent exactly. Under its own assumptions about the data
errors, each one's s.d. is right. The limitations below come from those assumptions and from the data, not from coding errors.

| Method | Fit | s.d. on realistic data | Broad patterns (1600 km) | Main caveat |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [DF](inversion-df.html) | Australia | 1.1–1.2× too small | not tested | s.d. too small with its settings fitted |
| [CM](inversion-cm.html) | Australia | 1.08× too small | kept (0.82–0.89) | weighted errors of unequal size treated as equal |
| [PD](inversion-pd.html) | Australia | about 3× too small | one level per domain | blind to variation inside a domain |
| [GCM](inversion-gcm.html) | global | right, except at sharp edges | lost (0.44) | one level and independent cells |
| [DF-GLC](inversion-df-glc.html) | global | right, except at sharp edges | kept (0.78) | noise held fixed |

: Summary. "Realistic data" means noise as in the real data, and for PD also VIS varying inside the domains.
Broad patterns: the fraction of the contrast of 1630 km tiles recovered with noise.
{#tbl-summary}

**The smallest pattern any of the mapping methods can see is about 200 km**, recovered at a third to two-thirds of
its contrast depending on the tiles and the noise. At 170 km (tested over Australia) nothing comes back. PD maps
domain levels only.

# How much of a pattern each method recovers

The fraction of a checkerboard's contrast that comes back, with noise. The local and global tests used different
tiles and different noise references (see below), so compare along a row within each table, not between tables.

| Square size | DF (one domain) | CM |
|---|---|---|
| 8° (900 km) | 0.85 | 0.86 |
| 4° (450 km) | 0.67 | 0.69 |
| 2.5° (280 km) | 0.66 | 0.68 |
| 2° (220 km) | 0.58 | 0.63 |
| 1.5° (170 km) | 0.03 | 0.05 |

: Australia: squares of latitude and longitude, noise measured against MF7. {#tbl-local}

| Tile size | GCM | DF-GLC (one domain) |
|---|---|---|
| 1630 km | 0.44 | 0.78 |
| 815 km | 0.77 | 0.79 |
| 407 km | 0.67 | 0.66 |
| 204 km | 0.33 | 0.30 |

: All continents: equal-area tiles, noise measured against MLI_SHA_2E. {#tbl-global}

# Why the methods differ {#sec-why}

- **At 200–800 km the data set the limit, not the method.** DF and CM recover the same over Australia, and GCM and
  DF-GLC the same globally. Given the same truths, tiles and noise over Australia, GCM matches CM at 400–800 km and
  trails it by 0.08 at 204 km. Better resolution needs better data (more of the field at high degree, or less
  noise), not a different method.
- **Broad patterns need a correlated field.** CM and DF-GLC model VIS as correlated over hundreds to thousands of
  kilometres, which carries patterns that the data constrain only weakly below degree 16. DF shares DF-GLC's model
  and should behave alike. GCM treats each cell as independent and pulls broad departures toward its one level.
- **The s.d. is right only as far as the error model is.**
  - GCM and DF-GLC weight the data by the full error model, so their s.d. is right whenever the truth is the kind of
    field they assume.
  - CM's weighting leaves weighted errors of unequal size, which it absorbs in one noise
    scale, so its s.d. is slightly too small.
  - DF fits 43 settings to 849 data, and the fitted settings make its s.d. too small. Sampling them helps only a
    little.
  - PD treats the errors as independent and each domain as uniform. Neither holds for real data, so its s.d. is the
    least reliable: the refit s.d. corrects for the first assumption, not the second.
- **The noise reference differs between the local and global fits.** The local fits measure the noise of LCS-1
  against MF7, the global fits against MLI_SHA_2E, which gives about a third more noise over Australia. For CM this
  alone costs 0.07 of the contrast at 204 km. Until one reference is chosen for both, local and global maps and
  their s.d. are not directly comparable.

# What applies to all of them

- **A small s.d. can mean "nothing seen here".** Where a pattern is too small for the data, the methods return a flat
  map with a small s.d., not a large one. This was shown for DF and CM; the global tests did not go to scales small
  enough to show it.
- **Sharp edges are blurred** unless the domains follow them, and the s.d. does not allow for the blur.
- **The resolution belongs to the data.** These limits are for LCS-1 at degrees 16–133 with its present noise. A
  model with more reliable high degrees would move them down; more noise would move them up.
- **A wrong ocean model** (global fits) lowers the whole map by about 4% and changes some continental margins.
